items.title: Periventricular gradient pathology is linked to ependymal reactivity and cell adhesion disruption in multiple sclerosis
items.author: Jo Anne Stratton
items.content: This study identifies ependymal dysfunction as a mechanism linking inflammatory cerebrospinal fluid to increased ventricular permeability and periventricular pathology in multiple sclerosis.

items.title: Spatiotemporal AI-based modeling of gene regulation and variant effects in the developing human brain using Seal
items.author: Olga G. Troyanskaya
items.content: Seal is an artificial intelligence framework that predicts the effects of regulatory variants in 802 brain cell states, revealing spatiotemporal gene regulation and pinpointing cell types and developmental stages associated with neuropsychiatric conditions.

items.title: An aging-sensitive secreted phospholipase confers neuroprotection and cognitive resilience
items.author: Amar Sahay
items.content: This study identifies a secreted phospholipase in the hippocampal dentate gyrus that mediates an aging-sensitive compensatory mechanism promoting cognitive resilience and neuroprotection.

items.title: A half-center oscillator regulates sleep pressure
items.author: Gero Miesenböck
items.content: Hasenhuetl et al. show that neurons innervating the dorsal fan-shaped body of Drosophila form a half-center oscillator, a circuit motif typically found in central pattern generators for locomotion. Here, this circuit generates slow-wave activity for the regulation of sleep.

items.title: 5-HT<sub>2A</sub> receptors in layer 5 pyramidal neurons mediate the neuroplastic but not the hallucinogenic effects of psilocybin
items.author: Yi Zuo
items.content: Psilocybin promotes and stabilizes new connections between neurons in the mouse cerebral cortex, especially after stress. Baker et al. show that 5-HT2A receptor signaling in layer 5 pyramidal neurons mediates this effect but is not required for a mouse behavioral proxy of hallucinations.

items.title: Symmetries and continuous attractors in disordered neural circuits
items.author: Haim Sompolinsky
items.content: Head-direction cells are far more disorderly than classical continuous-attractor models allow. Clark et al. show that this disorder is nevertheless compatible with these models and that the underlying connectivity matrix hides a circular symmetry.

items.title: Ring attractor networks go full circle
items.author: Srdjan Ostojic
items.content: Clark et al. demonstrate that heterogeneous data-driven models implement head-direction selectivity through the same dynamical principles as classical ring networks. In doing so, the authors reconcile biological realism with theoretical simplicity, unifying existing frameworks and broadening the space of connectivity structures to be searched in data.
